**Course source:** Day 2 §2–§3. **Running system:** Product, Order and User services.

## A client needs policy as well as an interface

The source discusses Feign configuration, request compression, log levels and internal execution. Those concerns apply even if Order is written in NestJS instead of Spring.

A remote-client design should specify:

| Setting | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| Deadline | Prevent one Product request from holding Order forever |
| Retry policy | Recover from transient failures without unsafe duplicate work |
| Authentication | Propagate an allowed credential, never secrets from untrusted clients |
| Logging | Observe latency and outcomes without exposing personal or secret data |
| Compression | Reduce payload bytes when size makes it worthwhile |
| Connection pooling | Avoid reconnecting for every request |

## Use the smallest useful example

~~~ts
const response = await fetch(productUrl, {
  headers: { 'x-request-id': requestId },
  signal: AbortSignal.timeout(350)
});
if (!response.ok) throw new Error('HTTP ' + response.status);
const product = await response.json();
~~~

A **350 ms deadline** here is a tutorial setting, not a universal production target. If Order has a total budget of 700 ms, independent sequential calls of 500 ms each cannot meet it. Timeout design starts at the user-facing deadline.

## Compression and logging

Compression is most useful on sufficiently large responses. It adds CPU work and complicates troubleshooting; tiny JSON objects may see no meaningful benefit. Logging entire payloads can expose customer information and increase storage costs. Prefer trace/request IDs, method, route template, status, elapsed time and selected service.

## How an HTTP-client proxy works conceptually

An interface proxy maps a declared operation to an HTTP method, path and parameter encoding, applies interceptors, selects a transport and turns the response back into a result or error. The course's Feign source walkthrough is valuable as an example of this pipeline, even if exact internals differ today.

## Practical review

Keep transport policy in ProductClient, not scattered across controllers. After moving clients behind one boundary, it becomes easier to introduce service discovery, tracing and circuit breaking without rewriting business decisions.

## Review questions

What failure does this technique address? Which state belongs to the caller and which belongs to the provider? What would you measure to confirm that it works?
